summary: A 1975 description of Network UNIX, a version of UNIX used as a mini-host on the ARPANET. It covers its standard input and output, Telnet, NCP, hardware and software needs, reliability and availability.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 681 describes a UNIX system adapted to act as a mini-host on the ARPANET. Programs use standard file operations for network connections, while part of the network software runs outside the kernel.

questions: unix on the arpanet mini host
how did unix connect to the arpanet
subtitle: How one UNIX system connected to the ARPANET while keeping network access in user programs.

tldr.problem: The UNIX system described in this RFC needed to use ARPANET protocols without putting all network functions into its resident kernel.
tldr.mechanism: It represents connections as special files accessed with ordinary open, read, write, and close calls. The Network Control Program is split between a kernel part and a swappable daemon process.
tldr.outcome: The memo documents a working Network UNIX implementation, its hardware requirements, observed reliability, and plans for further testing and services.

today: RFC 681 describes the Network UNIX implementation and its plans at the time of writing. Its report does not establish a later status for the system.

sections.title: Network Connections as Special Files
sections.content:
Network UNIX represents a host connection with a special file such as /dev/net/harv. Programs use the standard UNIX OPEN, READ, WRITE, and CLOSE calls to open the connection and exchange bytes.

This arrangement lets standard ARPANET protocols such as Telnet and FTP run as user programs that need be resident only when used. A program can also communicate with a network special file directly.
sections.plainLanguage: A network connection appears to a program as a special file. The program opens it, reads or writes data, and closes it with familiar UNIX calls.

sections.title: The Network Control Program
sections.content:
The NCP handles both message switching and host-wide control and status traffic. To limit the non-swappable kernel code, the implementation keeps a kernel portion of about 3.5K words and a swappable NCP daemon of about 8.5K words.

The daemon handles user requests to open and close connections and status traffic. It communicates with the kernel through a special file.
sections.plainLanguage: A small part of the NCP stays in the kernel. A separate process handles connection requests and status messages, and can be swapped like other user processes.

sections.title: System Experience and Plans
sections.content:
The report says Network UNIX had run full-time for about four weeks. It recorded three to four crashes a day at first, many attributed to hardware complications; after a hardware reconfiguration, the reported rate was one crash a day with two to three minutes of downtime. The sampling period was too short for dependable analysis.

The authors planned further bandwidth and load testing, additional parameters for OPEN, and later network mail, FTP, and remote job entry as user programs.
sections.plainLanguage: The system was still being tested, and the authors cautioned that their reliability measurements were not yet dependable. They planned more tests and additional network services.
